entry.description: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
entry.childHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.

stem.text: Read lines 5 to 9. Why did the Mole suddenly stop cleaning and run outside?

carriers.key: Spring outside was pulling at him and he could not sit still.

options.value: He had finished every job in the house.
Spring outside was pulling at him and he could not sit still.
His back and arms hurt too much to go on.
The Water Rat called him from up above.
He wanted to find the river he had heard about.
options.execution: He has not heard of the river — line 29 says he had never seen one in his life. The motive is supplied by the reader.

stem.text: Read lines 23 to 27. What does the way the Mole treats the rabbits show about him?

carriers.key: He is so excited that he will not stop for anyone.

options.value: He is frightened of the older rabbit.
He is so excited that he will not stop for anyone.
He is a cruel animal who is always unkind.
He is rushing home to get his dinner.
options.execution: Dinner is nowhere in the passage, and he is going away from his house rather than towards it.

options.value: He is sorry at once for knocking the rabbit over.

stem.text: Read lines 56 to 62. The Mole says, 'Oh, it’s all very well to talk.' What does this show about him?

carriers.key: He did not know how anyone could get across the river.

options.value: He did not know how anyone could get across the river.
He thought the Water Rat was being unkind to him.
He did not want to be friends with the Water Rat.
options.execution: A wish not to be friends is supplied; line 61 has his whole heart going out to the boat.

options.value: He was too tired from his walk to move.
He knew all about boats but did not own one.

stem.text: Read lines 66 to 67. What does the last thing the Mole says show about his day?

carriers.key: The whole day had been full of things he had never done before.

options.value: He was hoping the Rat would let him hold the oars.
options.execution: The sculls are the Rat's at line 66; the wish to hold them is supplied by the reader.

options.value: He was still frightened of the water.
The whole day had been full of things he had never done before.
He was already wishing he was back in his own house.
He had been in boats before, but never one as fine as this.

stem.text: Mr Bingley said no to the Bennets' dinner. Read lines 9 to 12. What reason did his answer give?

carriers.key: He had to be in London the next day.

options.value: He had promised to dine with Lady Lucas instead.
He did not want to meet the Bennet daughters.
options.execution: A wish to avoid the daughters is supplied; lines 5 and 6 have him hoping to see them.

options.value: He was busy planning the courses for a dinner of his own.
He had to be in London the next day.
He had gone to London to gather a big group for the ball.

stem.text: Mr Bingley's answer upset Mrs Bennet. Read lines 13 to 16. What was she most afraid of?

carriers.key: That he would keep moving about and never really live at Netherfield.

options.value: That he would keep moving about and never really live at Netherfield.
That her dinner had all been cooked and would now be wasted.
That he had gone to London to look for guests for the ball.
That the girls would have to meet twelve strange ladies.
That Mr Bingley did not like her daughters.
options.execution: A dislike of her daughters is supplied; the passage gives his reason as business in town.

stem.text: Read lines 36 to 41. The writer suddenly says: 'What a contrast between him and his friend!' Why is that sentence put there?

carriers.key: To make the reader notice how differently the two men were behaving.

options.value: To tell the reader that the two men had fallen out.
To show that Mr Bingley was cross about something.
To show that the writer likes Mr Darcy the better of the two.
options.execution: A preference is supplied for the writer, who states the contrast and takes no side in it.

options.value: To make the reader notice how differently the two men were behaving.
To show that the two men were really rather alike.

stem.text: Read lines 41 to 43. The writer says: 'His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world.' What do these short, sure sentences do?

carriers.key: They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.

options.value: They prove that Mr Darcy really was the worst man alive.
They show that the writer had run out of things to say about him.
options.execution: A motive is supplied for the writer; the shortness is doing the room's certainty, not his.

options.value: They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.
They show that Mr Darcy had at last made up his mind about something.
They tell us that Mr Darcy said nothing to anybody all evening.

stem.text: Elizabeth had to sit down for two dances. Read lines 47 to 48. Why?

carriers.key: There were not enough gentlemen for all the ladies.

options.value: She did not feel like dancing that evening.
Mr Darcy had refused to dance with her.
She wanted to listen to Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley talking.
options.execution: A motive is supplied; line 48 has the overhearing happen because he stood near enough, not because she arranged it.

options.value: There were not enough gentlemen for all the ladies.
Her eldest sister was dancing with Mr Bingley.

stem.text: Elizabeth hears Mr Darcy's words herself. A friend does not tell her later. Read lines 47 to 50. Why is that a good choice?

carriers.key: The reader hears the unkind words at the very moment Elizabeth does.

options.value: It shows that Elizabeth enjoyed listening in on other people.
options.execution: A taste for listening in is supplied; line 48 has him standing near enough for her to overhear.

options.value: It shows that the room had almost emptied by then.
The reader hears the unkind words at the very moment Elizabeth does.
Mr Bingley had planned for her to hear his kind words about her.
It shows that Mr Darcy was speaking loudly to the whole room.

stem.text: Read lines 51 and 52. Mr Bingley says to his friend: 'I hate to see you standing about by yourself in this stupid manner.' What is Mr Bingley trying to do?

carriers.key: Get his friend to join the dancing.

options.value: Tell his friend off for being rude about the ladies.
Get his friend to join the dancing.
Ask his friend to leave the ball and go home.
Make his friend feel sorry for the ladies who have no partner.
options.execution: Pity for partnerless ladies is supplied; the speech is about his friend and no one else.

stem.text: Read lines 53 to 56. Mr Darcy says: 'Your sisters are engaged.' What does 'engaged' mean here?

carriers.key: They have already promised their dances to other partners.

options.value: They have promised to marry somebody.
They are busy and cannot be spoken to.
They are standing and talking with Mr Bingley.
They do not want to dance with Mr Darcy.
options.execution: A wish not to dance with him is supplied; line 54 says nothing about what the sisters want.

options.value: They have already promised their dances to other partners.

stem.text: At the end, Elizabeth turns what happened into a story for her friends. Read lines 70 to 73. What does this tell us about her?

carriers.key: She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.

options.value: She has completely forgiven Mr Darcy.
She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.
She wants her friends to feel sorry for her.
options.execution: A wish for sympathy is supplied; lines 71 and 72 give her a lively, playful disposition instead.

options.value: What Mr Darcy said did not bother her at all.
She thinks Mr Darcy is a fine, handsome man.

stem.text: Read lines 15 and 16. The girl said there was 'more scope for imagination' outside. What does 'scope' on line 15 mean here?

carriers.key: Room for the mind to work.

options.value: Somewhere cooler than the waiting room.
A quiet spot away from people.
options.execution: Invents a reason for staying outside; the girl gives imagining as her reason.

options.value: Room for the mind to work.
A tool for seeing far away.

stem.text: Why does Matthew wish Marilla was there? (lines 24 and 25)

carriers.key: He finds this sort of trouble hard to face alone.

options.value: He knows Marilla is the shy one of the two.
He finds this sort of trouble hard to face alone.
He hopes Marilla will send the girl straight back.
options.execution: Supplies a motive the passage never gives; line 62 leaves all of that until later.

options.value: He wants Marilla to drive the horse home.

stem.text: Matthew decides to take the girl home. What does this decision show about him? (lines 59 to 63)

carriers.key: He would rather be kind now than face a hard talk.

options.value: Marilla had told him what to do in this case.
He never makes a decision by himself.
He would rather be kind now than face a hard talk.
He had always hoped that a girl would come.
options.execution: Gives him a wish the passage never states; line 61 still calls it a mistake.

stem.text: In town Beauty says 'I had a good bait'. What does 'bait' mean here? (line 14)

carriers.key: A feed and a rest.

options.value: Something used to catch a fish.
A long wait outside, with nothing to eat.
A trick played to make him go on.
options.execution: Invents a purpose; nothing in the line suggests he was tricked.

options.value: A feed and a rest.

stem.text: What did John say they would have to do? (lines 29 to 31)

carriers.key: Go back to the crossways and round, six miles further.

options.value: Drive slowly over the tree where it lay lowest.
Wait by the wood until the storm had passed.
Go back to the crossways and round, six miles further.
Unhitch Beauty and lead him home on foot.
options.execution: Invents an action; line 31 says the horse is fresh, so they drive on.

stem.text: Look at what the master does on the bridge. Then look at what he says at the hall door. What does the writer want us to understand? (lines 36 to 38 and 62 to 63)

carriers.key: The master punished Beauty for the very thing that saved them.

options.value: The master punished Beauty for the very thing that saved them.
The master knew that Beauty was right to stop on the bridge.
Beauty was too frightened of the water to cross the bridge.
The master had wanted to test whether Beauty would obey him at all.
options.execution: Invents a purpose; line 37 has him simply telling Beauty to go on.

stem.text: What did the master and John work out on the way home? (lines 54 to 58)

carriers.key: That going on would probably have drowned them all.

options.value: That Beauty had been badly trained and needed more work.
That the gatekeeper was to blame for the broken bridge.
options.execution: Invents a complaint; the passage gives them no blame at all.

options.value: That going on would probably have drowned them all.
That they were lucky the wind had lulled when it did.

stem.text: Beauty repeats what the people say, word for word. What does the writer keep reminding us at the same time?

carriers.key: He gives us their words exactly, but says he cannot follow them.

options.value: That Beauty is too frightened to listen properly.
That the people never speak to Beauty at all.
That Beauty repeats the words to show off what he knows.
options.execution: Invents a motive; the narrator's remarks are about what he cannot do, not what he can.

options.value: He gives us their words exactly, but says he cannot follow them.

stem.text: A whole semi-circle of people stands round while Uncle Podger works. What does the writer show by this? (lines 26 to 29)

carriers.key: A tiny job has taken over the whole household.

options.value: The family are eager to learn how to hang a picture.
options.execution: Invents a reason for standing there; line 26 says only that they are ready to help.

options.value: A tiny job has taken over the whole household.
The family were too busy to watch him properly.
The picture is very heavy and needs several people.

stem.text: What does Aunt Maria say she would like to do next time? (lines 49 to 51)

carriers.key: Go and stay with her mother while the job is done.

options.value: Ask Uncle Podger to let her hang the picture instead.
Go and stay with her mother while the job is done.
Send for a man to come and do it properly.
Hide the hammer so he cannot start at all.
options.execution: Invents a plan; her words are about leaving, not about stopping him.

stem.text: Uncle Podger begins by telling them to leave it to him. He ends by saying some people would have had a man in. What does the writer show by this? (lines 6 and 7, and 61 to 63)

carriers.key: He thinks of it as a success, exactly as he did at the start.

options.value: He has learned, as he did not know then, that the job was hard.
He is pleased, and glad they all helped so much at the end.
options.execution: Invents gratitude; at line 37 he calls them fools and at line 52 he blames them.

options.value: He thinks of it as a success, exactly as he did at the start.
He is boasting to them, and hiding it, because it went so badly.

stem.text: Reuben returns a cardigan whose owner has left. Later he puts his own named jumper in the charity box. What does the writer show by this? (lines 11 to 14 and 29 to 33)

carriers.key: He keeps the rule for everyone else and breaks it for himself.

options.value: He stops taking care by the end and forgets what he set out to do.
He keeps the rule for everyone else and breaks it for himself.
He could not tell whose the jumper was, so he put it in the box.
He thinks the jumper too worn for anybody to want it back.
options.execution: The cover story he gives at line 47 is about next year's fit, not about wear.

stem.text: Miss Bhatt looked at Reuben 'for a second or two longer than the answer needed'. What does this show? (lines 46 to 49)

carriers.key: She does not believe his reason, but lets it stand.

options.value: She is waiting for him to say sorry for the mistake.
options.execution: Invents a demand; at line 49 she folds the jumper away as he had it.

options.value: She has not understood what he said.
She does not believe his reason, but lets it stand.
She is cross that he has wasted the afternoon.

stem.text: Reuben put a cardigan in the returns box even though its owner had left. What does this show? (lines 11 to 14)

carriers.key: He would rather try to return a thing than give it away.

options.value: He did not know the girl had left in Year Four.
He was working faster than Ilya and made a mistake.
He wanted to keep the cardigan for himself.
He would rather try to return a thing than give it away.

stem.text: Read lines 16 to 19. What does Roberta's reply show about her?

carriers.key: She puts the work first and keeps the garden for later.

options.value: She wants to see the garden before starting work.
She is annoyed with Phyllis for talking about the garden.

options.value: She puts the work first and keeps the garden for later.

stem.text: Read lines 29 to 33. Why does the dog run up to Jane?

options.value: It had been frightened by the fall.

options.value: There was nobody else nearby that it could fetch.

carriers.key: He rates people by whether they can play his games.

options.value: He is jealous of the notice that Lucy will get tomorrow.

stem.text: Read lines 33 to 35. Why does Maggie shut her eyes tight?

carriers.key: She wants Tom pleased with her more than she wants him fed.

options.value: She is afraid that Tom will take both of the halves himself.

options.value: She is sorry for Tom having the smaller share.

stem.text: Look at lines 10 to 14. What reason does Jim give for staying hidden?

carriers.key: He alone held the lives of the honest men.

options.value: He was just about to jump up.

options.execution: A plausible reason for listening; lines 10 to 14 never give it.

options.value: He alone held the lives of the honest men.

stem.text: Look at lines 38 to 42. Why has Hands had enough of Captain Smollett?

carriers.key: Smollett has driven him hard for a long time.

options.value: Hands wants the pickles and the wine in the cabin.

options.value: They are standing off and on like a blessed bumboat.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. What does Jim keep doing while he lies in the barrel?

carriers.key: His body cannot move, but his mind goes on working things out.

options.value: His nerve holds while he hides, but it breaks once the moon rises.
He tells us he would not have shown himself for the world.

stem.text: Look at lines 25 to 29. Why does Tom ask Ben what he calls work?

options.value: To make Ben doubt that painting a fence is work.

stem.text: Look at lines 30 to 33. Why does Tom ask whether a boy gets such a chance every day?

To make the job sound like a rare treat for a boy.

stem.text: Look at lines 32 to 37. What is Scrooge doing in these lines?

stem.text: Look at lines 40 to 44. What has the moor got in it besides stone?
